Next time, I'll try their stir fry dishes - or even some of the prepared dishes in the window look pretty good. My only complaint would be that the place smelled a little funky, but what place in Chinatown doesn't? It's a part of the charm.

December 26, 2019 Penn Station New York, New York Chinatown is an old section of Manhattan, and yet the enclave holds new surprises every time I visit. I visited a Chinese apothecary looking for one item, a shop on Grant that also housed an acupuncture clinic. The man advised strongly against the one Chinese herb. However, I purchased a bottle of a male vitamin that I believe has lessened my arthritis. I am walking with diminished knee pain and with an extra level of energy. It could be a placebo effect. It could be an effect of plenty of curry with last night's dinner. It could be an effect of downing copious amounts of vitamins and D3 from Trader Joe's. Who knows? I'll just keep taking these items and see how I feel. And when walking around Manhattan, every little bit of flexibility helps. I paused for dinner at 218 Restaurant, a narrow shop with five tables and roast pigs and roast ducks hanging in the windows. I could have gone exotic and ordered the jellyfish. Instead I picked the creature comfort of an old favorite, Curry Chicken, served up in minutes. I always wonder why so much Curry Chicken remains after the rice dwindles, but I just finished up the tender chicken and sauteed vegetables without the rice. I'm sure if I followed a recipe I might come up with a nice meal. But I'm doubting I could duplicate the tenderness or the textures of the dish. I pulled out my PayPal card and was surprised when the waiter declared, "Sorry, cash only"! I asked after a cash machine. "Yes, sir, a Chase Bank has one two blocks away". A man at least twenty years my senior, surely the manager, walked out to the street with me. He pointed it out to me. "Do you see it"? I left my coat at the table to reassure him that I would return. However, did I even hold a thought that I could dine and dash at a Chinatown restaurant? One of those waiters probably could sprint and find me before I reached the Bowery Subway Stop. I was on my honor. They probably have to send people to that ATM ten times a day. Who runs a restaurant without a credit card machine? Many traditional restaurants in Chinatown only take "cashee". I was annoyed, however, because that added ATM fees to the cost of my Chinatown dinner. Where do people think cash comes from if not from ATMs with fees? As I left, a woman approached me, light plastic bags hanging upon her neck and arms. She might have been my age, dressed in shopping bags. Maybe she was collecting these light but useful bags. She didn't look like a bag lady, but what Chinese family would allow an older woman of the family to roam around Grant Street like that? I could see the owner staring out his window at the interaction, only partially concealed by the hanging collection of roasted meats. She smiled. "Cashee, please". I shared a dollar. She turned and walked up to the window, close enough to fog it. She might have been choosing her dinner. The meat sliced off the roasts can be had by the pound for a third of the price of a dinner. I walked over to Bowery and made my way up to the East Village.

The staff was friendly and was eager to answer any questions we had about the food. As for the food itself, it's not only your typical Chinese food. While they have the usual General Tso's chicken and beef with broccoli, the majority of the menu is made up of Chinese dishes with an Indian flair like fish chilli Masala and chicken Manchurian. We started with chicken dumplings and shrimp pekora as appetizers, and went on to beef Manchurian and beef chilli Masala with egg rice for our entres. The beef Manchurian was one of the best beef dishes I've ever tasted - spicy but worth every drop of sweat while eating it. Finally, stuffed as we were, our waiter talked us into having their special dessert, Faludah, which is like nothing I've ever had before. It's a mixture (I think) of yogurt, vanilla ice cream, pomegranate, grapes, almonds, and some type of noodle. Yes, noodle. It had other ingredients, but I won't even venture to guess what they were. Every single Berry on my dessert was perfect, not a hint of age, no black, no mush, no mold and all sweet. You might wanna say it's luck, but not dead winter. Plus they're open 7 days a week.

Personally, I love to try different foods from around the world. A friend took me to Awash for a late lunch/early dinner before seeing Blue Man Group for my birthday. I don't understand how more people are not aware of Ethiopian food. It is beyond delicious!! I relied on my friend for suggestions, because I am not familiar with the way food is served there. You pick your meat, and a side, and then prepare yourself for an amazing experience. They offer a hot drink, Barbajada, which is the most amazing combination of coffee, milk and chocolate. I can not even describe how smooth and yummy it is. It isn't sweet, but it isn't bitter, and honestly, writing this review, I wish I had one of those drinks right now. The food is served on a large plate, and everyone eats from the plate. Now, culturally I believe you eat with your right hand,(I asked my friend, so I did not offend) but they do offer a fork at every seating when the food is brought to your table. My friend suggested Awash Chicken. Each large plate comes with potato, carrot and onion sort of stew, a lentil side which is spicy, but not hot spicy, more like a warmth that spreads slowly over your palate like a blanket on a cool fall evening, and chopped kale which is strategically placed in two locations on the plate, seasoned in a way to cleanse and refresh your senses as you eat. Your vegetable side is placed on your platter at your table on two sides, and your protein goes right in the middle. Then you take a roll of bread place it on your side plate, and use pieces of that to take the food and eat. This dinner encourages conversation and an opportunity to connect with the person or people you are dining with. The seasonings are amazing, the food is beyond delicious. The only drawback were the restrooms. They are small, and I did not use them (the ladies room was not in service). Also, you must go down a few stairs so it may be very difficult for anyone with mobility issues, and it is not wheelchair accessible.

I've dined at Awash (East Village location, only) numerous times and have always enjoyed the experience as both the food and the service have always been terrific - until now - and after last night's experience, I don't think we will be returning. Upon entering, we stood at the front of the restaurant waiting to be seated for at least 5 minutes while the only server/hostess/busboy was busy at the "bar." Once seated, we realized quickly that the menu had changed, especially the combination platter we usually ordered, I was wondering if this was a sign of new management or a new chef? Instead of being a set menu, the combination plate now allows you to chose what items you would like, however, you are given less items than were previously included (it used to be one beef, one lamb and one chicken dish, but now the combo only includes 2 meats). In addition, your options are on the back of the menu, not with English descriptions, so you have to flip the menu back and forth to figure out what you want. More than 10 minutes passed before the waitress came to take our orders and bring water. She asked if we were ready and I told her yes, I believe so - but when I looked up, she was gone and took another 10 minutes to return. Once the order was placed it was almost 30 minutes before it came out of the kitchen, and when it did arrive, it wasn't good. The special kitfo (which we ordered in addition to the meat combo) was flavorless mush. The meat felt as if someone smashed it into burger patties and forgot to season it. The lamb stew (Beg Alicha) was incredibly tough, chewy and also lacking in flavor. The red lentils (Misir Wat) were under cooked (i.e., still hard) and had only a hint of flavor. The collard greens (Gomen), which is usually one of my favorite vegetarian Ethiopian dishes, was another disappointment. It was dull and flat without the freshness and bright flavors I was expecting. The Special Tibs (beef) was the only dish with any flavor, but even that felt like it was missing "something." Nothing that was supposed to be spicy was spicy. Things (like the special kitfo) that usually have visible jalapenos (like it should) had tiny minuscule chopped up bits, instead, which meant none of the befits of flavor, texture or heat from the peppers. It was a fight to get our water glasses refilled and another to get the check and then more waiting to get the check picked up and returned to us. We were there for over 2 hours, but only spent about 20 minutes of that time eating. No, I don't think we will be back again.

Bazar Tapas Bar and Restaurant has a very rich menu. The dinner menu is classy. I usually order Bazar Patatas Bravas or Pan Con Tomate. The Wild Mushroom Croquettes are great, too. Brunch is good, too! Go for 3 Eggs Any Style, Chorizo Shakshuka, or Bazar Patatas Bravas. Lunch? Easy! Pappardelle y setas or Royal Prawns. The tapas are on a whole new level, rivaling the finest in the whole of New York! Literally, any one of them is excellent! My favorites are the Char­Grilled Octopus, Crispy Brussel Sprouts, Pan Roasted Wild Mushrooms. The PEI Steamed Mussels are great too! And who said wine? Or sangria? Their red sangria is excellent! You can also pick from some excellent Bloody Mary, Mimosa, and Bellini! However, if you don‘t know what to pick, just go for the House signatures! They are out of this world!

I was meeting up with a friend for a Saturday brunch. Since I'm still not comfortable doing any indoor dining, I searched specifically for restaurants that had outdoor dining spaces, and Chama Mama popped up. Neither one of us have had a whole lot of experience with Georgian food, so we decided to check it out. Plus I had another friend who had been raving out about this place, so I was excited to try it. I made ressos via Yelp (SUPER easy!) for 12:30 in the afternoon. First, they take your temperature, and then you are led to a back patio. But not before you're treated to the smell of freshly baked bread in the back - which by the way is surrounded by glass windows, so you can see them in action. The indoor space is quite large and looks pretty cozy too but like I said, I will save that for non-Covid times - if we ever get there again. The backyard was very pretty - decorated with lights, vines, and pumpkins for the season. However, not all of the tables were exactly 6 feet a part, so I was a bit paranoid there. Since there were a few things my friend and I wanted to try, we decided to just split everything. We started with the Kashi soup (beef tripe and shank broth and enriched with the garlic and milk). Our waiter was really nice and knew we were sharing, so he offered to put the soup in separate bowls for us. I'm really glad we split this because it's a very rich soup. I don't know if I could have had an entire bowl to myself, especially if I wanted to try some of the other food. I didn't love the soup (probably because of all the richness of the cartilage) but it was very comforting on a chilly day. I also liked that they give you extra milk and fresh garlic on the side, so you can adjust to your taste buds accordingly, which I did. Next up was the Adjaruli Khachapuri (traditional open-faced khachapuri with our blended cheese, topped with an egg). I've had this once before at another Georgian spot a while back but this one was definitely better. The bread was crusty but soft (if that makes sense). It is pretty heavy since it's basically just a bunch of butter and cheese. I was only able to eat maybe a quarter of it. This would probably be best shared amongst four people, especially if you plan on eating other things. Finally, we shared the Kabab Beef and Pork (House blend of beef and pork wrapped in Lavash (flat bread) and served with Chama Mama Mint). This was AMAZING! The meat was very tender and flavorful, and I didn't even know I like lavash bread! Especially with the kabab. It was like a neat, compact little sandwich. Overall, it was a great experience. Our waitress seemed overwhelmed at times, brought wrong orders to our table, didn't let us taste the wine before pouring the bottle, giving us our check before we'd asked for it, and getting a few other minor things wrong. All of this could have been overlooked if the food were amazing, but sadly here, too, the restaurant fell short. The khinkali were nice and quite tasty actually. I think any chef should be embarrassed to present this to a customer, especially at that price. The roasted chicken, on the other hand, was actually quite good: juicy and flavorful. We also tried the salads, of which one was pumpkin. This was fine, but tiny portion and nothing terribly exciting. The eggplant, though, was quite good. Still, very small portions for the price. Overall, I have to say I am just disappointed, probably because I had such high hopes for what is really flavorful and exciting cuisine. My goodness - NYC has been missing out on one of the world's culinary masterpieces. Thank you, Chito Gvrito for gracing us with a taste of Eastern Europe. For two people ordered a total of 1 big plate, 2 appetizers, and a small plate + dessert to end a superb meal. (Yes- we are big eaters! :D ) Each plate was special and unique on its own. With each plate that were brought out, the flavors became more complex and delicious! - Adjaruli (Cheese bread)- Freshly baked bread stuff with cheese and an egg was a great way to start the meal - Aubergine rolls (eggplant in walnut sauce)- This will now be hailed as my favorite eggplant dish! The sauce mixture of walnuts, garlic, and fenugreek was to die for. I do not know if this was an authentic way to eat it, but I managed to save some parts of the cheese bread to soak up every last bit of that sauce. - Country potatoes & mushrooms- At first, this appeared to look like a simple potato and mushroom sautee, but the sweet and tart plum sauce on the side pulled everything together. - Chkmuleri (Chicken) - This dish and the eggplant was stiff competition for me in terms of the best dish of the night! This is no ordinary chicken and it was definitely not in an ordinary sauce. If you like that garlicky and fragrant essence, you will not go wrong with this dish !!!

LOVELY FOOD isn’t the full tale at any Michelin-starred restaurant, I concluded after a meal at lower Manhattan’s Crown Shy during the pandemic restrictions still in place during early 2021. Our party of four was seated in a yurt set amid towers on Pine Street, an adaptation by the restaurant owners to the restrictions on full occupancy. The flapped, khaki structures on a calm street were playful and novel, and the cuisine was very nice, in a hearty fashion. The servers were engaging, welcoming and accommodating. But something was lacking, and I concluded it was the busyness, pampering, skilled efficiency and architectural splendor I have come to expect of a restaurant at this level. Great eateries rely more heavily on the front-of-house magic than I had understood!

Crown Shy may be my favorite restaurant in New York. Some higher end restaurants have either shut down or been phoning it in during the pandemic. Thank you so much, Crown Shy, for providing a fine dining experience that is delicious, warm, contactless and safe during the pandemic. I wanted to have an intimate birthday dinner, but since indoor dining is closed in NYC, outdoor dining or takeout are the only options. Not wanting to dine in my apartment another night, I sought warm outdoor dining options and I am so pleased I found Crown Shy. The cozy yurt decorated with fir branches, graffiti art work, fur lined chairs, blankets, heat lamp and music creates the perfect atmosphere, pure magic! Then the food is amazing, the flavors and textures are a party for the senses. Crown Shy more than deserves its 1-Michelin star!

We came for the special yurt seating, and all four of us were in agreement that this was an experience not to be missed! The food, the service, and the ambience were all perfection. What we love most about the food was it didn't try to be overly fanciful in a ridiculously artistic kind of way, it was just good food made to perfection with flavors that I can still remember a month later. We found it well deserving of its Michelin star, but was also the kind of place that wasn't just a bucket list tick to do once; rather it's a place I will come back to again in the future.

The first time we went to Crown Shy last year, the food and service were both a bit inconsistent, but we could tell that there were some really amazing dishes... perhaps they had an off night (and they were super busy). Last night, we went back a second time for "outdoor dining" in one of their "Village Yurts" and EVERY DISH hit it out of the park. My favourite thing about our meal last night was how different every dish tasted - sometimes with tasting menus, there will be this overarching flavour profile which can get a bit boring, but that definitely wasn't the case yesterday. I also loved the attention to detail in the yurts - they had some light music playing and that really made a huge different for me. Sometimes with these outdoor dining spaces in NYC, the "outdoor" spaces are dead silent and can feel stuffy. However, Crown Shy really took the time to make everything beautiful with the faux fur throws, the blankets, and some chill music. Love the waitstaff's matching vests and beanies - nice touch, and very on brand. :) Way to crush outdoor dining, Crown Shy!

Definitely had some kinks to work out early on but they have gotten it done. CBR quesadilla, fish and chips, shrimp po-boy and fried pickles all done perfectly today. Service was excellent. Glad that I gave it another shot.

Overall nice experience but watch out for spotty service when things get busy.

Lunched today at the Crown Shy restaurant. But what you really want is terrific food, and emerged well paced. Terrific tasing, fresh, warm olive infused bread, yummy pear appetizer, and some of the best chicken (tangy and just the right juicy-tenderness) I've had in NYC. But the piece-de-resistance came last, as it should, in a fantastically concocted apple sorbet. My only complaint is they've not yet arranged to produce and sell the sorbet by the quart! Hopefully soon ;) Can't recommend Crown Shy any more highly (and a Michelin star to boot!). Can't wait to go back.

Having read lots of good reviews I was looking forward to trying this new restaurant out. Things didn't start off too well though. I arrived about a minute or two late and one of the greeters took me to the bar where my husband was having a drink. Not quite sure why this was necessary as there were plenty of tables available. I ordered a non-alcoholic cocktail which was nicely done by one of the bar tenders and quite interesting. 15 minutes later though and still none of the greeters came to seat us. My husband went back outside to remind them that we were still waiting to be seated whilst I stared at all the empty tables...a few minutes later one of the greeters deigned to come seat us. Still not quite sure what the delay was as there were plenty of greeters at the front desk. Given the menu is very limited in choice I was expecting every dish to be pretty much perfect, but taste wise it was fine but overly pretentious in presentation. If they had been charging less it wouldn't be so bad but going for higher end pricing for not higher end food was rather disappointing. Ironically, the bread was good and that was a freebie. The decor is kind of odd too in that you have stone tables but almost cafeteria like chairs. The open kitchen doesn't help in adding to that cafeteria feel. I know there's a trend for open kitchens but I think they missed the mark a bit in the design of the restaurant. The noise levels were loud due to all the hard surfaces, but we were at least seated in a corner so didn't get as much noise and could just about hold a conversation without the need to bellow at each other. It wasn't packed though and I expect it'd be pretty noisy when it is. Overall a little disappointing and I doubt I'll be paying a second visit.

Crown Shy fuzes a casual atmosohere with fine dining. It is elegant but not pretentious. The food is simple yet elegant and creatively presented. We had the chicken which came well cooked and succulent, the oysters were fresh and had a wonderful seasoning, our salad was packed with flavour. I was celebrating passing an exam and when we arrived the hostess and waitress both mentioned it and just that little detail makes the night stand out be an experience I will always remember. This is a very special place and if you can you must try it out.

Restaurant for amateurs! Trying real hard to become a name in the scene, with all its undeserved hype, this restaurant is for the 30 something trying to discover NYC. Any real local will notice the unrefined service and lack of detail in their dishes. After living in NYC for 15 years, it is hard for me to take any recommendation seriously, however, giving this place a try ended in serious disappointment. From their bread service of a butter soaked loaf and mismatched what seemed like sour cream cheese (ugh) as condiment to oddly soaked tagliatelle pasta, this restaurant is a no win win from all angles. The staff lacks serious maturity and the knows of how to deal with a discerning NY crowd. After my unfortunate taste of their lack of professionalism and sincerity, this will be my one and only try at this amateur restaurant. It will not be long before they become that lunch spot during the day and abandoned by night. Farewell crown and don't be shy to up your game in a competitive market!

Oh man. No one wanted to love this restaurant more than me. I live in FiDi and am always envious of all the interesting restaurants opening in other neighborhoods. But I have to say, my boyfriend and I had SUCH a frustrating and disappointing experience there yesterday. The timeline of our meal pretty much speaks for itself. We had a reservation for 7:45. We came super hungry because we had read so many good things about the food and planned to feast. We were seated at 8:10. A few minutes later our server came to take our drink orders. We put in an order of gruyere fritters right away. He didn't smile ONCE the entire evening. Not once. Which is especially weird because my boyfriend and I are very smiley and upbeat. When my boyfriend said he had a shellfish allergy and asked if the carrots were cooked in the clams or if the clams were on the side, the server mumbled the answer without making eye contact and had a vibe like "ugh I don't have time for this." 8:25 the bread came. Delicious. Wish it would have come much sooner. 8:42 red snapper crudo and fritters come out. Fritters are barely warmer than room temp, so much like room temp mozzarella sticks or fries, they were a little underwhelming. Crudo was delicious though on the small side. At this point we realize we're still incredibly hungry so we're hoping to flag down our waiter to ask for more bread. We don't see him anywhere for a long time. 8:49 we finally ask the woman who refilled our water glasses if we could have more bread 8:57 more bread comes 9:16 our entree (Carmelle pasta) finally comes, also close to room temp. Still no sign of our server, so we didn't have the option to ask it to be heated up a bit. It was still delicious, and I imagine it would have been even better if it was hot. We had come in with the intention of trying at least one dessert, but by 9:30 we were so frustrated and desperate to leave we just asked for the check. (Server finally reappeared around that time after his hour long disappearance.) TLDR: we came ravenous to a 7:45pm reservation at a restaurant with a ton of hype and glowing reviews, and we were served a lukewarm entree at 9:16pm. SO sad. I feel like we could have had a five star experience if only we had good service and the food came out on time. Oh well.... Maybe we'll try again once the restaurant has had enough time to replace this grumpy dude.

Was looking forward to eating here since it opened, but the experience was less than great. It took over 40 minutes for the bread to come out and we had a 20-30 minute wait from the last appetizer to our entree course. My entree (short rib) was room temperature and on the cold side when it finally came. While it was very good, it should have been hot or at least warm. It was obvious the entrees sat and waited for some time vs. coming out fresh. I mentioned this to the waiter half way thru me eating it (since we couldn’t find him and I was hungry) and he did offer to replace it but we didn’t want to wait any longer as we’d been sitting for 2 hours at this point. Thought something would have been done to compensate (not expecting a free entree) for a cold entree but nothing was done. Additionally, our neighbors were extremely drunk, loud and spilled red wine on my fiancé (the couple did take care of our drinks which was very nice). Multiple staff members apologized for their behavior after they left but couldn’t ask them to behave while they were seated. 3 stars because the food/drinks were awesome but the experience was inadequate.

When you work in FiDi, you're surrounded by some of the best lunch options the city has to offer, but Dig Inn beats them all. The customer service at this location in particular is what truly keeps me coming back. Despite the length of the line during lunch hours, the crew at Dig Inn finds time to make the experience personal. Today I commented to the cashier that the Chimichurri sauce had changed and she glowed as she confirmed that it had. She then mentioned it to her colleague who came over and excitedly discussed the difference in ingredients. The whole conversation took about 2 minutes, which is a meaningful amount of time to dedicate to a customer during lunch rush hour, but it felt like a bespoke, boutique experience. The crew is also incredibly skilled at building relationships with their guests. They routinely greet repeat guests by name, with a smile, and offer to prepare your regular order. Lashandra and Tiffany, who usually work the food line, and Shaquana, who works the register, are some of my favorites. They always brighten my day and I see how they put a smile on the face of so many.

I had a great dining experience here the other night. I came with 5 other friends. Everything we ordered was delicious. We started off with drinks. I wanted the Secret Lover, because I'm big lychee fan, but they didn't have the ingredients for it. Instead I ordered the Gin Flower Crush which has St. Germain Liqueur and was really good. Other drinks ordered were the Pom Pom Margarita, the Liquid Passion and plum wine. Everyone said their drinks were good. I got a glass of the plum wine. It was my first time trying it and it's a little too sweet for my preference, but it was good. We got a bunch of starters for the table including the summer roll, basil fried rice, Thai fried chicken wings (my favorite), spicy chicken bao buns, Thai peanut dumplings, slow cooked pork belly, gyoza and grilled pork skewers. Everything was honestly so delicious. We were already starting to get full from just that, but there was more to come. Our entrees included a sashimi platter, the chirashi platter, ramen, Pad Thai, duck red curry, pork shoulder, Chang Mai noodles, tuna steak and my order which the crispy mock duck which everyone agreed was one of the top meals. It was so good and you honestly wouldn't know it was vegetarian or even if you could tell, you wouldn't care, because it was so flavorful. It comes in a chili basil sauce or garlic. I got the garlic sauce and was very happy with my decision. The tuna steak was another pleasant surprise. The tuna was cooked so well and was really delicious. I didn't expect to like it as much as I did. For dessert we got the matcha mousse, mocha ice cream and the anmitsu parfait. The matcha mousse was our least favorite. The color of it looked so cool, because it was so green; however to get it that green they needed to use a lot of matcha powder which was very overpowering. The mochi ice cream was good if you like mochi. It's not my favorite, but I don't hate it. It's chewy, but I like ice cream so I tried a little. The best dessert we all agreed was the anmitsu parfait. There are so many elements to that dessert. It has agar jelly, vanilla ice cream, rice mocha, corn flakes, red bean paste and brown sugar syrup. As you eat you find more and more things inside and we were all like little kids eating. Overall, the meal was excellent, the service was great and the atmosphere of the restaurant is nice. I would definitely go back if I was in the area. I say this because I don't frequent Brooklyn that often.

Dock Asian Eatery is a beautiful spacious restaurant in Bushwick. They serve Japanese and Thai food with ease and grace. The staff was gracious and so attentive. The bar was beautiful. We sat upstairs in a loft dining area. It felt like you were in exotic treehouse, dining in the tropics. We shared the following. Drinks: Sapparo draft beer, iced green tea and Echigo stout. The stout was refreshing and had a hint of coffee. Sashimi special- this was so good and fresh. Esp for a restaurant serving both Thai and Japanese food. Reading the reviews, people complained about the quality of the fish. There were no complaints here. The salmon was fatty and unctuous. The yellow tail was fresh. The tomago was soft and melted in our mouths. The scallop was sweet and so tender (this was my favorite piece). The botanical ebi head was creamy and fried to a great crunch. The otoro was very creamy and satisfying. The chirashi bowl- this was also fresh! And the sushi rice had bits of sweet pickled vegetables and mushrooms to add texture to the rice! I liked the lean tuna, the shrimp and the salmon roe. The seafood ramen was good- very rich flavors. I loved the added poach egg. The noodles were springy. The shrimps were good, the clams were plump but the broth was a little salty. Chiang Mai noodles- this was slightly spicy sweet curried noodles (a version of Kaho Soi). I love the noodles! The curry was good, slightly sweet from coconut milk. The chicken chunks were a little overcooked and dry. Beef Yakitori- good chunks of beef. It was a little dry but very flavorful. Toro pork (pork belly)- This was the best Yakitori. The juicy crispy pork belly went perfectly with the yuzu pepper paste. This was a wonderful amazing mind blowing bite! Shiitake Yakitori- this had a smoky flavor. It was a little undercooked and dried. Dessert: Coffee Jelly- concentrated coffee jelly topped with vanilla and coffee ice cream. The coffee tasted like nitro drip. It was very strong. It tasted like an affogato but with totally different textures. Anmitsu Parfait- this had chewy delicious mochi with corn flakes, vanilla ice cream, red bean paste and topped with brown sugar syrup. This was my favorite dessert! I loved the mochi and all the blends of textures and varying levels of sweetness. Matcha Mousse- green tea on the outside, vanilla mousse on the inside and paired with an adorable mouse-like yuzu sorbet with a mint leaf as its ears. This was my 2nd fav dessert. This was an great meal with varying flavors and strengths. I would definitely reorder the Sashimi special, the Toro pork Yakitori, the anmitsu parfait and the matcha mousse. @snackchatnyc

I signaled the male waiter and he apologized and took it back to the kitchen. And that took you an extra 40 minutes..For our entree, Lapin ordered the Stroganoff ($25) and I ordered the Grilled Branzini ($29). Now, I feel like there were just messing with me. I got really annoyed and then after much arguing the "young manager" said he would remake my dish but last time I got the same food again. It was a small but plump piece of fish that took another 45 minutes to get to me. It came with decently tasting mash potatoes but no sauce with mash or fish. Lapin said it would be fine, but I am not chancing it after eating raw fish. I was soo hungry, I had to eat around it. I told them they had to comp'd us for dessert because saying "sorry" is no longer an excuse. But after starting to feel ill, I said I don't want to see any dessert or fish anymore. The manager snarkily replied "they don't serve fish dessert". I asked them for 2 glasses of Prosecco which was decent. I had sip and felt more sick (could be from exhaustion and an empty stomach). We celebrated my birthday this past weekend at Blue Hill at Stone Barns and had a disappointing experience. First, we really enjoyed the service level and knowledgeable staff. We mostly interacted with a server named Evan and he was friendly and helpful. The wine that your sommelier recommended for us was amazing and everyone at my table loved it. Everyone also enjoyed the broader experience of the décor and music selection that accompanied the courses. Unfortunately, we were extremely disappointed with the meal itself. We had high hopes for the food after eating at Blue Hill in NYC and seeing chef Johnny Ortiz's background, which includes positions at two excellent restaurants (Alinea and Saison) and a semi-finals spot in the "Young Gun" competition. In our opinion, the courses were too similar (too beef forward, not enough vegetables) and lacked flavor and complexity. For many of the courses we felt like there was a lack of seasoning (for example, no spiciness, despite the dishes having a Southwestern origin). These views were shared across everyone in our dining party of 4, and we all have different backgrounds. It pains me to put this in writing after meeting the chef Johnny because he was extremely nice and down-to-earth. Unfortunately, we are still very disappointed 4 days later. I personally feel very guilty for inviting 3 people who graciously spent $330 / per person for a meal where they did not enjoy the food. When we informed the restaurant that we were dissatisfied, they did nothing to make it up to us. I am weary to ever visit Blue Hill again and I implore you to take your business elsewhere.

Our table opted for the chef's tasting menu with 2 optional additions. I felt that many ingredients repeated themselves in the different dishes and things started to seem familiar. Overall, we all thought the portions were very small. After the 6th course my stomach started feeling odd. Could I have eaten something bad? Luckily, no. It was then that I realized I was simply just hungry and my stomach was growling, which I found to be super funny! And before you make some kind of unwarranted judgment that I'm some kind of plebian, let me assure you that I am no stranger to fine dining and Michelin-starred experiences. Service was good, with staff quite attentive and polite. Until something must have went off the rails. It was a busy evening, and there was a 40 minute dead zone between our 4th and 5th courses. We pointed this out to our server after about 20 minutes of waiting and she apologized saying that the kitchen was very busy. Yes, I could see that judging by how packed the restaurant was, but it was a weak excuse for a restaurant that prided itself on its service. At the end of the evening, I just didn't feel satisfied. Were my expectations too high or maybe I caught Blue Hill on an off evening? Maybe. Even my friend who was the repeat customer felt our evening fell short. He tried to make light of the situation by saying, "I hope you enjoyed your appetizers at Blue Hill. Now, let me take you to dinner!"

This was probably the most disappointing restaurant experience I have ever had. I had wanted to go to Blue Hill in NYC since I saw the Chef's Table series. Totally inspired by the philosophy of the restaurant I convinced my boyfriend we would have dinner there on one of our three nights in NYC. It was my boyfriend's first time to the city, so I made sure to book a couple of good places in advance - Blue Hill being one of them. My boyfriend is coeliac. I informed the restaurant in advance so that they would be able to accommodate him on the set menu. We have done this many times in other high-end restaurants, so I didn't think this would be an issue, especially in NYC. The waiters were aware of the dietary, however they weren't able to share what the GF option would be "The chef will create something special" was the response. It is frustrating receiving this response, as it makes it seem that they do not have a clue. In addition to this, the wine bottle we got was corked. We informed the waiter/sommelier and they kindly took care of it and replaced with another wine which was delicious. Once the food arrived, it was extremely average. We ended up waiting about an hour between the second starter and main. The main that arrived was so disappointing that although I love food and never leave dishes uneaten, I couldn't finish it. Not to mention the below average GF option my boyfriend got - chickpeas in the starter sauce with a couple of pieces of chicken. The combination of the lack of attention to the special diet, the tasteless food and the extremely long wait, was shocking for the 190 USD we paid for the meal, plus wine. The waiters did what they could to make up for it, however the kitchen really let them down. Never ever will I recommend this place to anyone.

I am saddened to report that my wife got food poisoning here. I got it too, but to a way lesser extent. It's a shame, as we had been looking forward to dining at Blue Hill for a long time. We were in town on vacation and celebrating our friend's birthday. We think the poisoning was caused by the greens from the carrot, which was the first course. I will say that our server, Mary, was awesome. She was friendly, fun, informative, etc. The experience as a whole was good, although we've definitely had better food for more reasonable cost. But when my wife started violently throwing up about 6 hours later, our view understandably changed. It got so bad that I had to take her to urgent care the next morning to get treated by a doctor. It was then that I called Blue Hill to tell them what had happened. To their credit the manager I spoke with, Cole, seemed to take our situation seriously, telling me he would inform the chef, etc. and expressing sympathy for my wife's situation. At this point, if you were in our position what would you expect a high-end, Michelin-star rated restaurant to do? Give your money back, right? I mean, it's not like it's Chili's and you spent $50. We spent almost $500... to get food poisoning! At first I didn't say anything about the money, thinking that of course they would offer to refund at least part of our bill. Cole, who was also very nice, said they had a 48 hour procedure to follow and they'd need to see if anyone else got sick that night, etc and that he would call me back in two days. I said I totally understand and I look forward to speaking with him again. He never called. Again, a restaurant of this caliber... I felt like it was adding insult to injury. I called him five days later. But I don't want to paint this as dealing with nasty people or having a big screaming fight. It wasn't. Cole was very polite and apologized for not calling. We had a very civil, respectful conversation. However, he said my wife was the only person to get sick and therefore they felt that maybe she got sick from somewhere else. Now, is this possible? Sure. From our perspective though, there was nothing else she or I ate that day that would be a suspect for causing food poisoning. It does seem highly more likely that carrot greens from a farm could have not been washed thoroughly. And that just because no one else got sick doesn't mean that the greens on HER plate didn't cause HER to get sick. Cole then told me there was nothing else the restaurant was willing to do for us because they felt sure the food poisoning wasn't from them. Although, he did say he hoped we'd come back and give them another chance. Ha! The thing is, it's not about the money. We chose to go there, as we have many other expensive restaurants over the years. We knew what it would cost and we decided to go. Not that we can afford this kind of dinner more than maybe once a year, but still. It's about customer care. A person comes to your restaurant and believes they got sick from your food. If I were the restaurant, especially a high-end one like this, even if I thought you may have gotten sick elsewhere, I'd say, “let me at least refund your wife's meal. I'm sorry your experience here was tainted.” I mean, what does that really cost them? All it does is make them look good, make me feel cared for as a customer, and de-escalate the situation. Again, I do understand where they are coming from and their point of view. I just think in terms of customer relations, PR, whatever you want to call it, there's a right way to handle these kinds of situations where with minimal output you can make everyone walk away feeling better. Instead, they chose to make my experience even worse. UPDATE: After contacting upper management and posting this review, the owner of the restaurant emailed me personally to apologize and provide compensation. He was very gracious and he handled the situation as it should have been handled from the start. So for that, I am grateful.

I planned a big engagement weekend to propose to my fiancee. I was planning to propose during a hike, followed by a fun celebratory meal at Blue Hill. We made a 1:30 p.m. reservation at Blue Hill and provided our credit card for the $258 per person charge. We emailed Blue Hill and the hotel to arrange a photographer for the actual proposal, and to arrange roses and a whole engagement plan. It was a really special day for us. We drove up, went on a hike, got engaged, and everything was great. We were planning to head over to Blue Hill for the surprise, romantic meal to top off the engagement. As we getting ready, I checked my email. I had received a notification that our reservation (for less than hours later at this point) had been "Cancelled" in the Blue Hill automatic system (the cancellation email is attached; it is dated March 4 at 12pm for a 130pm reservation, and lists the scary cancellation policy at the bottom). We had also received an email and voicemail from the director of Guest Relations saying that, due to a storm that had knocked out their power, they were cancelling our reservation. Blue Hill has a policy whereby they charge the $258 per person dining fee if the customer cancels within 48 hours. We called the person who emailed us back, and she said that she was sorry but they were closed, asked if my fiancee had said yes (again, they knew we were getting engaged that day),and asked if we could reschedule for another date. She was almost nonchalant about it. We told the person we spoke with that we understood they couldn't control the weather but wished we had known earlier (the storm was Friday night and was totally finished by Saturday at noon; our meal was Sunday at 1:30pm; and they notified us Sunday at 11am). We could have canceled the rental car, hotel, and everything if they'd told us Friday they would not be open Sunday rather than waiting until two hours before our meal to was to begin. I told my fiancee I was sorry and that we could celebrate privately in NYC. We then drove the rental car back to New York City, grabbing sandwiches along the way. I could tell my fiancee was slightly disappointed that there was no grand meal, but she seemed to understand that I had tried my best to make it a special day. We were a bit taken aback because Blue Hill's staff definitely knew we were getting engaged that day (we had emailed about photographers, etc.); they knew we planned our engagement - a very special moment in our lives - around the reservation to eat at their restaurant. There's more to the story but the character limit prevents me from saying more - the key is that, in my opinion, others should be cautious about planning big events at Blue Hill at Stone Barns.

This place is bustling and smells amazing. There's a "best of New York" award on the inside, and based on my experience it's clear why. I had macaroni pie, a pumpkin + bhagee roti, a sour sop drink, and some doubles for later. The roti skin itself is tender and soft, and choosing to mix the slightly sweet pumpkin with the potato + greens that was the bhagee turned out great. (So note: you can mix fillings from their roti board.) The macaroni pie has a nice hint of smokiness to the flavor, and is satisfyingly creamy and cheesy. I'm not normally a sweet drink person, but I took a chance on the sour sop and am glad I did. It was deliciously milky and tropically fruity, and just sweet enough. As a vegetarian who grew up on German food, I really love cuisines with a lot of naturally occurring vegetarian dishes, and Caribbean definitely hits that spot. Gloria's not only has the wide variety of vegetables, curries, chickpea and bean dishes that are veggie hallmarks of Caribbean cuisine, but also has soy crumbles and tofu as options if you're looking for some additional veg protein. Though there were a *lot* of people in line, the wait felt reasonable for what I ordered, and was definitely worth it. There are a handful of hightop tables and chairs, but this definitely seems like a takeout spot. Grab some tasty takeout from Gloria's and find a nice bench on the parkway to enjoy it!

I've lived in NYC all my life and I remember when this place was one of the hot spots in Manhattan. I'd never been, in its heyday but when I read a review about the current chef in New York Magazine, I was intrigued by her confidence and modern menu. It was my boyfriend's birthday and we usually go to a nice restaurant for our birthdays. My boyfriend is very no-nonsense and doesn't like to pay exorbitant sums of money for vegetables that we can cook at home. That being said, I told him let's give this place a go. I made reservations and told them it was his birthday. We were greeted at the front by a host and hostess who wished him a happy birthday. Those little extras are kind of fun on your birthday. Our table was not ready yet so they suggested that we have drinks at the bar. We found space at the bar and ordered a drink each. When our table was ready, we were seated and our waiter came over to greet us. When I looked online at reviews, Gotham had mixed reviews. There were some very good ones and some very poor ones. The good ones mostly reflected the service, which was remarkable. The dishes we ordered however were disappointing. My boyfriend ordered the pork cheek appetizer, which to me was a dressed up version of pork and beans. No subtle nuances of flavor there. We both ordered the porcelet entree and although the microscopic baby brussel sprouts and tiny tamarind figs were present, the pork on my plate was dry and devoid of flavor. Our waiter asked us what our opinion was and I was honest. My boyfriend says his tasted good but mine did not. It simply did not taste. The waiter did bring over a dish that I believe was a cabbage with some type of cous cous, which had more flavor than the main course. We had an apple dessert which was tasty. My most enjoyable experience was with the Somalier who recommended a lovely wine. Our waiter was extremely professional as was the support staff. The truly sour part of the evening was when the bill came and there was over $150 worth of drinks attached to our bill that we did not have. When I pointed this out to the waiter, he apologized and handed me a pen, asking me to circle the items that did not belong to us. I did so and they were promptly removed. However, it left me wondering how many other patrons do not catch these little mishaps. In summary, great staff but the fare should live up to the hype and the prices.

My experience here will stay with me for the rest of my life. I actually mean that. I am not a foodie-type person, and never spend money on food. If it’s healthy, I will eat it. Food as fuel is my general approach. But I went there a year and a half ago to have meat for the first time in my life (since being a lifetime vegetarian), as a sort of sacred ritual to initiate this new phase of my experience, and it was honestly mind-blowing for me. I took it slow, the whole thing lasted 4 hours, my eyes were closed much of the time, and honestly the plants and animals I gratefully took into my body that night put me into a deeply altered state. I have friends that just went for the first time recently, and they confirmed my experience. They, too, found themselves in an altered state. I recently went back with my family, and had an amazing time. Their outdoor structures during covid are something you really just have to see for yourself to understand how much attention and creativity they put into every aspect of what they do. These are generous people, who really care about and live what they share through their food experience. When you go, you are supporting a wonderful family, an ecosystem, and a network of foragers, hunters, and others who put restoration of local ecosystems first. I highly recommend this place if you are looking for something really special. When you go, I would recommend thinking of it not as a meal, but as a sacred experience of communion with life.

Oh my stars. Five of them, take them all. This city never ceases to amaze me. The outdoor structures they’ve built are so beautiful and private and very safe, and we embarked on a multi course sensory experience, and opted to do a drink pairing, and our minds and tastebuds were blown. This is forest to table, forage to table, wild to table realness. Everything is foraged from the North East and everything is so complex yet so simply presented. Everything had intention and love in it. The bill was not cheap, but I was so happy to invest in this beautiful experience run by the most loving, passionate, and hard working couple. Don’t come hungry (small portions), but come curious (each dish is out of this world and unique). Perfect for a romantic date, celebration, or dressing the f*ck up and treating yourself to something transcendent. I love this city, and I love Honey Badger.

It wasn’t looking like a great Christmas. Unable to visit my family for the first time in my life and in a city I’ve only called home for two years, things seemed foreign despite their familiarity. Presents didn’t arrive on time. Zoom didn’t replace family time. It was a bleak end to a bleak year. Then, on the 26th, I had the opportunity to take solace at Honey Badger. My partner and I were warmly ushered into a cabinesque structure lining the street in front of their establishment. On a silk curtain strung across the restaurant’s windows played classic movies featuring New York skylines not seen since our grandparent’s generation. Our feet and cabin were warmed quickly by the provided heaters. No sooner had we sat down when our waiter, who also happened to own the restaurant along with his amazing partner and their daughter, brought us a pallet cleanser that was aptly described as wild; the spilanthes plant. Used by Native Americans to cure toothaches, the plant has a mild anesthetic effect, almost like a tingle on your tongue. The curiosity of this plant was a foreshadowing of the delights to follow. Each course we had built upon the last. Inside our well-built yet makeshift abode, we dined on roast duck, oysters, fish baked in coconuts, and chestnut soup. I’m a simple guy. A home cook meal is almost always preferred to a fine dining establishment. And yet the meal spoke to me in a way I’ve never experienced. Perhaps it is because I’m an aspiring outdoorsman (and because Honey Badger sources everything from local foragers and farms). Perhaps it's because it's Christmas. Whatever the reason, somehow, sitting in that tiny little cabin with my gorgeous girlfriend, having carefully constructed course after course described in elegant details made this stranger in a strange land feel like he was home, if only for a meal.

Frankly, it felt almost too casual/hip to pay half a grand via venmo (not to mention the credit card points that we couldn't get from this meal). At this point, the atmosphere was really starting to slip. My girlfriend and I were both hungry and had no concept of how much longer we would be waiting for our food. Even worse, as we sat there tired, hungry, and increasingly frustrated, the owner's(?) child was sitting in the kitchen "playing" a flute very loudly above the otherwise pleasant music. Why she was allowed to do this is completely beyond me. It was loud, erratic, piercing, ....and just utterly unpleasant. Still, we sat there, helplessly waiting for our third course. At no point did the waitstaff check in on us to see how we were doing or let us know that the food would be delayed. After ANOTHER 45 minutes the third course finally came. Some sort of meat with seagrass on it. Unfortunately, after the first bite, I decided it would be a hard pass for me. This course was so salty that it was hardly edible. My girlfriend, who unlike me had not had lunch that day, scarfed hers down and then asked if she could have mine "It's awful, but I'm just so hungry" she said with a pained look on her face. I decided we had had enough. Rather than sit there for presumably another 45 minutes, we would just cut our losses and go eat elsewhere. I waved over the waiter and politely asked for the check, telling him we'd have to be on our way. Another server brought the check, and I was slightly surprised we were charged for the entire tasting menu even though we only had three out of the five courses. (I understand that you pay for the entire menu, not per course, but I had secretly hoped the staff would pick up on the fact that they had made us wait almost a full hour between each course and we had completely lost our motivation and enjoyment - In my view, they could have at least comped the drinks) At no point was there any acknowledgment by the staff that the courses were taking an inordinate amount of time to come out. While waiting for course three, I even went to the Honeybadger website to see if they made mention of this somewhere (they don't). We also were not asked whether everything was to our liking at the end or I could have told them that it wasn't. Alas, with other guests right next to us, I was not going to dispute the check or make a scene. So, a full 2 hours and 15 minutes after sitting down, we ended up paying almost $200 for a small salad, a small soup, the saltiest meat we have ever tasted, and a glass of wine. I'm embarrassed to say we ended up at the $1 pizza joint across the street just for the sake of actually getting some nourishment. This is a long review that I wouldn't ordinarily write, but I am just so utterly disappointed by my experience here. Slightly angry, definitely annoyed (what's with the flute playing??), but mostly just sad and disappointed. I was so very eager to come here (my girlfriend had wanted to go elsewhere and I had to convince her to come here instead) - we were ready to have a great evening and celebrate my birthday, and ended up feeling like we wasted two hours being hungry and burned 200 bucks. It's not even about the money, it's just a special evening that got ruined. I really hope our experience was the exception - It looks like other patrons are having great experiences, but based on tonight, I cannot in good faith recommend coming here.

Honey Badger is, without a doubt, the most innovative restaurant I've been to in my 64+ years on this planet. I've lived in NYC for almost all of my life and have been to many great restaurants here, around the U.S. and overseas, but Honey Badger is one of a kind. To begin with, the restaurant is the creation of a husband and wife team who built the space from scratch in a storefront on Fenimore St (right off Flatbush Ave). The physical space is both intimate and enchanting - totally unique - unlike the "cookie cutter" approach one tends to see in every "hip" restaurant in Brooklyn these days. All the details were conceived and executed by them; even the "background" music is tasteful and just perfect. What about the food? It's almost beyond belief. They source all their ingredients through a network of foragers and hunters. There's no factory farmed anything here. Everything they prepare has been obtained in the most ethical manner possible - by environmentally conscious people who work with nature instead of ravaging it. What they do with the raw materials is almost beyond belief and without precedent. I've never eaten more creative and delicious dishes prepared in a way that will absolutely blow your mind. It's like magic; some sort of alchemy! I absolutely recommend doing the tasting menu when you come here. Allow yourself at least 2-3 hours to fully appreciate the experience. The menu changes every night (depending on what they've received), but I would just go with whatever they're offering. You won't be sorry.

My friend's sister birthday request was for an Indian restaurant. Of course, my usual selection would probably be in the Curry Hill area on the East side but we were in Brooklyn. Prospect Heights to be exact and unfamiliar territory. We found Joy along the busy corridor of Flatbush Ave with lots of happy eaters inside so decided to give Joy a try. The casual restaurant but plain decor was an open room with tables and a small bar in the back. The restaurant was quite full and they politely asked two of the patrons if they would mind moving to a two top table for our group of six. The couple didn't have any issues and we graciously thank them. The menu had the usual selection of popular Indian selections and some that I haven't seen before therefore it is an automatic must try. The table ordered some usual favorites and some new like Samosas to start and Chicken Tikka Masala, Gobi Bhajee, Saag Paneer and Shagoti with lamb. Samosas was crispy without being to oily. Plenty of flavor and a slight heat afterwards. The Tikka Masala was a bit sweeter than I'm use to with a tangy tomato sauce. I always enjoy the Gobi(Cauliflower). I think the standout of the dishes was the Shagoti which the table agreed was very good. It had a slight heat, the lamb was tender and not gamey. The sauce was great not only for mopping but with the rice. The portions we thought was a bit on a smallish side but was still more than adequate for the table. I think if we were a bit hungrier we'd need to add one additional dish. I think when in the area this certainly will satisfy anyone craving Indian cuisine without taking the 5 train to the city. Joy Indian left us happy and ready for some after dinner fun in the neighborhood.

I won’t bother with the rest of the conversation/argument, but in the end we are very unhappy with our experience at Lorenzo’s and certainly won’t be returning. Because we are cheap? There is a pronounced preference for, fresh, seasonal and even raw ingredients over anything more obvious. This kosher (under supervision of the VHQ) in Rego Park, Queens focuses on the cuisine of the Republic of Georgia. This is one of the provinces of the former Soviet Union. We started going to Marani several years ago. They also do takeout and we have gotten takeout from them several times. Both when we ate in and took out, we enjoyed the food tremendously. Its one of my favorite restaurants. The wait staff is very good and is able to explain the dishes on the menu very well to people like me who are not familiar with their cuisine. The cuisine has lots of roasted meats, meat dumplings and hearty stews. There are some vegetarian dishes but its not a vegetarian oriented cuisine. There are some smaller appetizer items but primarily its large, filling entrees- I wouldn't go if you are not hungry. Marani is not cheap but prices seem in line with upscale kosher restaurants. Their is a wine, beer and spirits list. The basement of the restaurant is a different menu. It offers several diary dishes- various types of cheese pies . I had one once - it was great. My only complaint about Marani is each time I go there this diary section does not have any cheese pies for sale. Parking in the area can be hard to find. There are some parking lots not too far away. The restaurant is near the 63rd street subway station. If you like trying new and to those of us not familiar with the cuisine unusual dishes, Marani is highly recommended. February 2021 update- The restaurant has reopened for inside dining (at 25% of capacity). We have already tried it- its still great.

Along with the Family Store, this is the brightest gem Bay Ridge has to offer. The food is authentic, high-quality, and top-notch. Service is great, and the owner is a *very* good looking Polish woman). I have a fondness for eastern European food in general, and this restaurant definitely satisfies my cravings! A few small gripes: First, they should mix up the salads a bit because it gets monotonous to eat the same (excellent) 5 salads (beet salad, coleslaw, sauerkraut, red cabbage, carrot salad) each time. It's cool the first 2 or 3 times, but by your 5th visit here it's tiring. Maybe they should only give 2 salads and change up which ones you get. The 2nd gripe: while you're eating, they use Fantastic to clean the table next to yours with no regard about where the spray goes. It never fails -- I always get Fantastic up my nose and it ruins dinner for a few minutes. The last gripe is that they don't accept credit cards; but I suspect this is because they don't need to -- the food is so good that they can be cash-only and still turn a healthy profit. This a restaurant you *must* go to before you die. If you go only once, I recommend the Ukrainian Borscht and the Stuffed Kielbasa. Portion size is huge, but mostly because of the salads. You won't finish your dinner. Entrees average about $10. Here's the low down on the food. Soups: --------- Sauerkraut: A- Surprisingly good (who would think sauerkraut would be good in soup?). Tomato: B Not really their fault; I'm not a big fan of tomato soup to begin with. I'm sure it's good. Vegetable: B- Easily the worst thing on the menu. Has a metallic taste to it. Cucumber: A+ Ukrainian Borscht: A+ Both soups are perfection. If you order one of these, you will fall in love with it. Chicken Soup: B- Disappointing. Watery and not very interesting. White Borscht: A You get an egg and mashed potatoes with caramelized onions with it. Red Borscht with Croquet: B+ It'd be good tasting but a tad boring without the croquet (which is a little like chicken kiev). Red Borscht with Dumplings: B It would be good tasting but a tad boring without the dumplings. Barley: B- Sounded good. Unfortunately, a bit bland and lackluster compared to the borschts. Bean: B+ Very nice flavor. Spicy, thick, and hearty. Good for winter. Appetizers -------------- Mushroom and Potato Pierogi boiled): A- Spinach and Potato (fried): A- Delicious. I would recommend getting the sampler. 6 homogeneous pierogi is too much; diversity is better here. Boiled and fried are equally good. PETER TIP: Ask the waiter for more caramelized onions...they are DELICIOUS and the pierogi are even better with more onions. Blintzes ----------- Cheese: A Strawberry: A Blueberry: A They are perfection in the guise of blintzes. The Polonica does not serve dessert, but these dishes would definitely fill that void (but good luck wanting dessert after eating so much!) Other -------- Potato Pancakes: A Potato Cutlet: A Again, both dishes are perfection. I think you get 3 or 4 pancakes which are familiar if you've ever had fried latkes for Chanukah. The Cutlet is like a Godzilla-sized pancake. Entres --------- Meatballs: A- Beef Goulash: A Both delicious and masterfully cooked. The meatballs are a little like salisbury steak. Pork Chop (Breaded): B A little plain. Exactly the "chef's pork chop" minus the cheese. Chef's Pork Chop: A- The Pork Chop with cheese; the cheese definitely enhances the dish. Brizol: B A bit dry. Boiled Pig Hocks: C- Not their fault. I'm just not a fan of boiled meat period. Plus, hocks look a little strange to my Western eyes. They're feet. Very fatty and not very flavorful. I'm sure hock-lovers would like it. Fried Fish: A It may be sole, but you will NOT be disappointed. I promise you. Stuffed Kielbasa: A+ A heart attack waiting to happen, but easily the best thing on the menu. Boiled Cabbage: A Another perfect meal. Tasty chopped meat and rice inside well cooked cabbage leaves with a very savory tomato sauce.

BANGLADESH 🇧🇩 Eat the World NYC review: At some point around four years ago, the popular restaurant named Sugandha shuttered and the space at 483 McDonald Avenue underwent major renovations to become even more popular (and larger) Radhuni Sweets & Restaurant. The steam tables and all food were pushed to the back near the kitchen and the space was opened up for much more seating. As in other Bangladeshi spots in Bangladeshi neighborhoods around town, Radhuni feels like a community center at times, busy with men drinking tea and chatting or arguing. The steam table and counter might seem crowded and a bit of a fight, but the staff usually is friendly to those outside of the community and will make a point to help you. Just stand near the register and it will not take long. Feel free to ask questions about the food and come up with a good plan of action. Make an order, pay if they ask (sometimes you will pay after), and grab a seat. The water is already at the table and a small plastic cup will arrive with your selections if you have not been given it already. I can never pass up a good haleem ($5), and the one here is fantastic especially when you consider the price. Paired with a piece of naan ($1) fresh from the oven, it's an incredible meal. The dish is full of so many earthy flavors like wheat, barley, and lentils, but also fatty meats and spicy peppers. The dish is cooked for hours until it becomes thick and is easy to pick up with pieces of the bread.

At the site of this appearance, there is now a festival each year to celebrate the events. Back down here on Earth, this little bakery and restaurant is popular with livery cab drivers and other Ecuadorians inspired by their weekday lunch specials, excellent prices, and quick service allowing them to get back in their cars and back to work. A shrine in the front has dolls to (I'm guessing) represent the Blessed Mother, and some patrons say a prayer and touch her dress on the way out.

This turned out to be a lengthy review. Jump to the last paragraph if you just want a summary. I'm usually looking for a restaurant that has a variety of options to satisfy myself and my kids. Terrace definitely has a variety of food. There's your usual breakfast fare with eggs, bacon, English muffins, pancakes, fresh squeezed juice(!), and the such. For lunch and dinner, they have the typical American food options with burgers, chicken sandwiches, chicken fingers, wraps, mozzarella sticks, fries, onion rings, milk shakes, and so on... They also serve Mexican food like nachos, burritos, fajitas, quesadillas, etc. There were more options but the menu was too large to look through it all! I had an idea of what I wanted anyway. I did see a French onion soup that I was thinking I might come back for. There is indoor and outdoor seating available. We sat inside today. It's decorated with some lovely paintings in the front, a bunch of Marilyn Monroe pics in the next section and some other pictures I didn't get a good look at. The waiter brought our menus promptly. The food took at least 25-30 minutes to come out. By the time it got to us, the kids were half-way done with their shakes. I ordered a margarita that was not the best. My son got a plain cheeseburger with fries. My daughter got the chicken fingers with fries. I got an avocado cheeseburger deluxe with sauteed onions and waffle fries. The burgers were overcooked, but not dry. I took a tiny bite of my daughter's chicken fingers and they were tasty. After assembling my burger, I bit in. The burger was okay- not the best, not the worst. I added some salt and pepper to help it. My son didn't like his burger at first. I told him to try it without the bun and he ate it without further complaint. The waffle fries were great! We then tried dessert. My daughter got vanilla ice cream with fudge and whipped cream. My son got the churros with vanilla ice cream. I got the chocolate mousse and stole a little of my daughter's whipped cream😉. Neither of them finished because they were so full! Lol. The food was decent, but the dessert was wonderful! It was a beautiful Thursday afternoon. I noticed only 2 or 3 waitstaff on hand, who were nice. Although it wasn't very busy, I think they could have used a little help. There are 3 unisex bathrooms and 1 family bathroom. There's a 2-faucet sink outside the bathrooms, and a couple other paintings to decorate. There was music playing but I don't recall what it was. I think it was music from the '80-90's but not really sure. The atmosphere was nice. The food was acceptable. The dessert was great! I think it's worth another visit. Maybe I'll try the Mexican menu next, or the French onion soup & mozzarella sticks I was eyeing... 🙂

I've made several visits to The Bar Room over the past couple of years and I've never been disappointed. The classics (Tarte Flambe, Charred Avocado, Steak Tartare, Carrot Rillettes) are obviously great choices and worth having if you only get to make one visit. But on my latest visit I was astounded by just how great everything was. If I have a meal where one of the dishes is a Religious Experience, I consider myself lucky. But when I have a meal where dish after dish after dish is an R.E. (Yes, the Bar Room delivered on that)? I must have died and gone to heaven. Appetizers: The Shaved Fennel Salad (smoked salmon and grapefruit) was dressed perfectly and demonstrated solid taste and texture complexity in every bite. This is not just some fennel, salmon, and grapefruit thrown in a bowl and tossed with some dressing. It is ultra refinement of exactly the right pieces, sizes and quantity of fennel, with exactly the right pieces, sizes and quantity of smoked salmon (with equally top drawer execution of the smoking), with exactly the right pieces, sizes and quantity of grapefruit... dressed perfectly. That's a lot to say about one little salad, right? Yeah, but it was one heck of a salad. An R.E. White Asparagus Soup: ultra refined tastes and textures. Yes, I'm saying that about a mere soup. Morel Mushroom Fricassee: each bite was different: Sometimes subtle sweetness from the corn and sometimes interesting acidity from the pickled shallots, but always beautiful textures on the palate.Caviar Soldier: maximum indulgence. But every appetizer always has ultra refined tastes and textures (are you sensing a common theme here?). Entrees: I'll skip the entrees because they were all great. That's not to undermine them either. They are all worth having. Desserts: the menu seems to change fairly frequently with no one recurring signature dish. But trust me that this is a good thing, not a bad thing, and I don't mean that in a negative way either. Every dessert I've ever had at the Bar Room, bar none (pardon the pun), has been excellent. So why is it a good thing that they change the dessert menu relatively frequently? It's simple: It's practically a sport to see what incredible creations the evil geniuses will come up with next. Most recently, the Rice Pudding (rhubarb and jasmine ice cream) was mind blowing with ultra refined tastes and textures (I know, I know, I sound like a broken record). I recall a Sweet Potato Parfait some months ago, which on the surface sounded mundane, but was a religious experience. These are not sloppy, in-your-face sweet, throw it down on the plate, desserts cooked up by some pastry chef who is not the equal of the Executive Chef. These are ultra refined, complex tastes and textures that are the equal of every dish you've had leading up to the finale. Service: excellent of course. You wouldn't expect anything but warm, attentive, down-to-earth, sincerely friendly, and knowledgable from a place of this caliber. The wait staff, Somms, bus-people, runners were all consummate professionals. Tipping: I have to say that although it has taken some getting used to on my part, and although I know the front of the house doesn't like it, Danny Meyer's "Hospitality Included", No Tipping policy at all of his properties is a big bonus for the customer. In a traditional tipping environment, it's always awkward to know how much tip to leave on the wine portion of the bill vs the food. There is no need to go over the accolades that The Modern has received over time; three stars from the New York Times, a Michelin star, and several James Beard Awards since its opening in 2006 are enough to define the caliber of this restaurant. Diners should note that there are two separate dining areas in the restaurant, the less-formal Bar Room, which serves dishes a la carte, and the Dining Room, which requires diners to choose either the four-course prix fixe or the tasting menu. Signature items include the "Alsatian Dumplings", filled with a savory and tender rabbit-truffle filling and the Quail Baked "En Terre Glaise", a surprisingly intricate dish. The quail breasts are wrapped in grape leaves and baked in clay, a cooking method that's completely separate from the preparation of the legs, which are carefully seared. The protein is placed a top an assortment of vegetables, including morels and spinach, which have been cooked in a rich wine and cream sauce. If that were already not enough, the plate is finished off with a ring of Macaroni Grantiné, a concoction which Kreuther himself likens to mac and cheese. Regardless, any meal here is sure to be near-flawless, and a dining experience to remember.

My husband had the curry salmon which he enjoyed. The restaurant is still awaiting a liquor license so they could only offer mocktails and fountain drinks. I had the sorrel which was tasty but literally took two sips and it was done-for $4, the drinks should come in larger sizes. For dessert, we tried the cake which also tasted good but we couldn’t finish it because it was unnecessarily covered in a bunch of chocolate and caramel syrup which made it too sweet and was totally unnecessary. They syrup was not included in the description of the dessert. When I told my server about that, he said, “Oh, they just want to make it pretty”. My husband wanted an ice cream scoop to go with the cake however the menu lists gelato, not ice-cream. The server couldn’t really tell the different and insisted that it was ice-cream. He ended up not getting it because he didn’t want to have gelato. I have high hopes that The Simpson will be a great restaurant once they work out some of the kinks. Dinner for two here is pretty pricey considering no alcohol was consumed. Still, I would recommend that you give it a try. The customer service is good and the chef seems like a wonderful person though we did not get to meet him during our visit.

Veselka is an East Village institution, occupying the same cozy corner of Second Avenue for almost 7 decades while serving up hearty portions of Ukrainian comfort food. In the city for the first time in almost 10 months and looking to satisfy a pierogi craving, I decided to finally give this spot a try. Even at noon on a cold December Tuesday, a line was building for tables outside (either under a heat lamp or just at a table on the sidewalk). Shielded by a huge winter coat, I grabbed a table on the sidewalk. Service here is lightning quick: my order of Ukrainian borscht, a pierogi bowl with mushrooms, onions, dill, and sour cream, and a Lvivski lager all came out in record speed. Don't look for anything fancy here: this is solid Ukrainian cuisine. The borscht was just sharp enough, with bits of short rib and chunked beets while the pierogi (boiled, in this case, and filled with potato and mushroom) were expertly prepped with just enough dill in the mushroom and onion topping. In bygone times, Veselka ran around the clock. Here's hoping things pick up and they can return to feeding the masses 24/7 again soon.

Profiteroles and Chocolate Hazelnut Bar were the highlights. The restaurant itself was gorgeous to look at, mixing the original style and sophistication of the Palace Hotel with fresh and modern design. If it weren't for the chaotic staff, poor service, and tourist-y clientele, this would have been a lovely evening. The waiters lacked any formal training to serve in an establishment like that. There often seemed to be more waiters, hostesses, managers scurrying around than diners, one wondered why it took twenty minutes to flag the waiter down so we could order or witness why a neighboring table found it impossible to request their check. Not to mention the lady who was patiently waiting for coatcheck to find her coat. It almost seemed chaotic the action that was happening behind our seats. Sitting in the bar dining room is not advisable as well with the entrance to the lobby directly in the center of it. We had every tourist and staff member whirling by us as we dined on our $30 dollar pieces of salmon. Are waiters supposed to run when performing their tasks at a restaurant? And all the nervous and tense looks on the staff's faces did not add up to a pleasant dining experience. Apparently what we learned was that they had just opened up their fine dining, 5 and 7 course tasting dining rooms, hence the overwhelmed and unprepared staff. Deal with it. All in all, it's fair, alright, okay. The Palace is going to have a convenient and good restaurant for their guests. But I could never consider this a true New York fine restaurant. Just like the hotel's guests, this restaurant will just be a tourist.

Homerun debut! Visited this restaurant back in February the week they first opened. They did a good job re-purposing the old space (RIP Bishops Wells) and making it look more trendy and inviting. They were still working on obtaining their liquor license back then but I could tell from the beautiful rustic bar that they would draw a crowd during happy hour. BYOB so they let us bring our own bottles without any corking fee. Really impressed with the friendly staff. The owner (Jacques) interacted with everyone, even people passing by and reading the menu. He also asked for our frank feedback regarding our dining experience which I really appreciated. Our waitress was also very attentive, patient and personable. Very pleased with the food. In NYC, you can only count on one hand the Haitian restaurants whose food really slaps. Our table of four enjoyed about everything we were served. Fast forward to these COVID times, the food is still the star of the show. Their menu served both classic Haitian dishes and a few modern ones, vegan options as well. All gluten free. You gotta win Haitians with the rice first. Their Djon-Djon (black rice) is wonderfully moist and well seasoned, properly accompanied with peppers and onions. Their chef won me with the goat, tasted it both fried (Kabrit Boucane) along with fried plantains and pikliz and served broiled in a nice kreyol sauce. The lambi (grilled conch) came out nicely textured. My husband took a chance on the Bali burger made with Herring and loved it. This past weekend, we enjoyed their brunch delivery. I was given a colorful omelette served on top of a crispy waffle while the hubs had the fried chicken and waffle. All their dishes (even if delivered in a box now) had a beautiful presentation. Will continue to support their business. I'm honestly hoping they make it through this current storm. One of the few places on my list to have a flavorful meal with delicious cocktail when this is all over.
